1:
Clarke reports that the Hebrew and all the versions give the psalm to David, written when he was firmly seated at last on the throne, but that the Greek and Arabic prefix Haggai and Zechariah, making it a thanksgiving for the settlement after the captivity. Delitzsch takes those added names as evidence about the collection rather than the author, and holds that though the speaker of verse 4 must be a king, nothing favours David's hand: the psalm is composed out of David's soul, an echo of the promise in 2 Samuel. He notes the contrast with the psalm before, where praise was dumb before the heathen, and here the heathen kings sing it.

Augustine begins from the word confess. The title tells only to whom the psalm is chanted, so its first line must tell what it is about; and confession in Scripture runs two ways, of sin and of praise. The first is so familiar that whenever the words are heard our hands hurry to beat the breast — but was Christ a sinner, who said I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and revealed them to babes? That is praise, not sin. Spurgeon notices that the psalmist never says whose name he praises, as a man does not name the father or friend he is speaking to.

Before the gods is the real crux, and every reading of elohim is on the table. Clarke prefers in the presence of Elohim, before the ark, and lists the rest — the Chaldee before the judges, the Vulgate and Greek before the angels, the Syriac before kings — then turns on the angelic reading, urged as proof that angels in Christian assemblies carry our praises up to God. There is nothing like that in the text, he says: grant that elohim means angels, and the praise is still not offered to them, nor are they asked to carry it. Ellicott decides for before the great or the mighty. Henry takes it as princes and judges, of David's nation or others, observing that praising God is work the greatest of men need not be ashamed of, being the work of angels and heaven. Calvin allows either sense and prefers the angels, since the assembly is a heavenly theatre and one purpose of the cherubim over the ark was to teach that angels attend worship in the sanctuary. Spurgeon reads it as idols, and will not suspend his singing because images stand in front of him.

The second crux is verse 2. Henry takes it straight: the judgments of God's mouth are magnified above those of his hand, the wonders of grace exceeding those of nature, revelation discovering more than reason. Ellicott feels the strain: one would expect thy name above thy promise, and the Greek and Latin found the difficulty so great they wrote thy holy one for thy word. Clarke reports that all the versions read above all thy holy name, renders it himself that God has magnified his name and his word on every occasion, quotes Kennicott's paraphrase that he preferred faithfulness to his promise over the attribute of his power, and concludes that the clause may be corrupt.

The kings at the end divide them again. Spurgeon takes them literally and joyfully — kings have small care to hear the word, a little piety goes far in courts, and here is a double wonder: kings in God's ways, and kings singing there. Ellicott holds it against the parallelism to suppose heathen monarchs actually walk in righteousness; the line means they sing of the ways, compelled to acknowledge Jehovah's glory. Gill allows the same reading of the preposition; Clarke splits the difference, since they will admire the workings of providence even if they never unite with God's people. Wesley calls the ways his counsel and gracious providences.
6:
The turn at verse 6 is read as the whole point. Henry has God, who needs none of his creatures and can be benefited by none, overlooking heaven and earth to cast a gracious look on the lowly, while he knows the proud — knows them, but disowns them, however they pretend to his favour. He passes on Hammond's suggestion that this is the sum of the gospel the kings of verse 4 will hear: penitent sinners accepted, the impenitent cast out. Ellicott makes the same distinction out of the verb: Jehovah looks down on lowly and proud alike, but one look is gracious interest and the other merely marks men to be kept at a distance. He quotes the maxim that lowliness and humility are the court dress of God, and that whoever wears them pleases him well.

Spurgeon turns the sentence into an exchange. Because the lowly think little of themselves, God thinks much of them; low in their own esteem, he makes them high in his. The proud need no closer inspection: one glance from far off reveals their emptiness. Then he lists what God has refused — a Cain's sacrifice, a Pharaoh's promise, a Rabshakeh's threat, a Pharisee's prayer — and Nebuchadnezzar, who cried Behold this great Babylon which I have builded, and went out to graze with the cattle. His contemporaries go in the same file: men who boast of their culture and their freedom of thought and criticise their Maker are known from afar and kept at arm's length. Clarke says the same in a line: God beholds them at a distance and holds them in derision. Gill measures the height they are set against: above the earth, above the heavens and the angels, above the praises of his saints.

Verse 7 is a walk, not a rescue from one. Gill presses it: trouble is not an interruption of the way but the way itself, a road walked through to the kingdom, long but not endless. Henry notices that David, a great and good man, expects it, and reads the promised hand carefully — not stretched against the enemies to destroy them, but against their wrath, to set bounds to it, the other hand doing the saving. Clarke makes it a bargain with experience: he has tasted enough of that mercy to trust it into any trouble. Ellicott hears the twenty-third psalm behind the line, and allows the hand may be stretched upon the wrath rather than against it.

The last verse is a confidence that turns at once into a request, and Henry is careful about the order. Its ground is that God's mercy endures for ever — a hope of persevering rests not on our strength, which fails, but on that mercy, which does not, and it is well pleaded that since the mercy is everlasting the pleader may be an everlasting monument of it. The confidence does not supersede prayer but quickens it, and the expectation becomes the petition of the second half. Whatever good is in us is God's own handiwork, and will fail if he forsakes it.

What is to be perfected they divide over, each answering from his reading. Gill takes it first of the kingdom — God had made David king over Judah and would finish by setting him over all the tribes — then of the work of grace on the heart, gradual and certain to be completed. Clarke will not choose: the body, the soul, the work begun in it, the work for Israel, the evangelising of the world, none of them forsaken. Ellicott says the prayer's intention depends on where the psalm came from: if out of the troubles of rebuilding Jerusalem, it becomes intelligible and expressive. He renders the last clause not forsake but do not leave them unfinished. Wesley reads it as the deliverance, advanced this far by no human help.
